children: The Bank of Italy defended its application of international banking rules governing the classification of troubled loans, after regulatory findings at specialist Italian lender BFF
triggered a plunge in its share price.

The shares are down by more than 80% year to date, weighed down by regulatory pressure which has led to the bank being placed under special administration as credit losses mounted, and raised the prospect of a potential sale.

BFF shares slid 18.7% on Wednesday, a day after the lender — which provides financing to public-sector suppliers by buying invoices before they are paid — published quarterly results in which it forecast that a capital shortfall was likely before 2028.
BFF took steps earlier this year to fix a capital shortfall that emerged with first-half earnings.
Milan prosecutors opened an investigation into alleged false accounting at the lender in February. BFF said at the time that it was cooperating with the public prosecutor's office.

A Bank of Italy audit earlier this year led to the appointment of two special administrators at BFF as the capital shortfall emerged after the central bank found issues in its factoring and lending business, including in the way loans were classed, BFF said in March.
The Bank of Italy said in a note on its website late on Tuesday that in applying the rules in recent years, it had stepped in when it saw that banks did not adopt them properly.
For example, some banks counted incorrectly the days of delay in an overdue payment or classed a loan as performing while also booking late-payment interest, it said.

"The Bank of Italy, when it uncovers irregularities in how loans are classified and regulatory capital calculated, asks banks to address the shortcomings and then checks that the measures are effective," it said.
"The supervisory measures are proportionate to the nature and seriousness of the issues and can include early intervention steps if conditions set by law apply."
BFF said in its results statement on Tuesday that it was in talks with US private equity firm Cerberus about a potential investment.
